title: HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication
summary: This informational RFC describes HMAC, a way to check that a message is authentic and unaltered by combining a secret shared key with a cryptographic hash function such as MD5 or SHA-1. Its strength depends on the underlying hash. HMAC is widely used in other protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: HMAC turns a standard cryptographic hash function, such as MD5 or SHA-1, into a check that a message has not been changed. Two parties that share a secret key compute the same tag, so only someone who knows the key can produce or verify it. How strong the check is depends on the hash function underneath.

questions: what are ipad and opad in hmac
how long should an hmac key be
subtitle: How to turn any standard hash function into a keyed integrity check that only key holders can produce.

tldr.problem: Two parties that share a secret key need to check that data sent between them has not been altered, and they want to build the check from hash functions that already exist and run fast in software.
tldr.mechanism: HMAC hashes the message twice with the secret key: once with the key mixed into a fixed inner pad, then again with the key mixed into a fixed outer pad.
tldr.outcome: The construction treats the hash function as a replaceable building block, so a stronger hash can be substituted later; RFC 2104 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 6151.

facts.label: Truncation t
facts.value: At least half the hash output and at least 80 bits

today: RFC 2104 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted, so it is still the definition of HMAC. It has been updated by RFC 6151.

sections.title: Why a Keyed Hash
sections.content:
A message authentication code (MAC) is a tag that two parties compute from a message and a shared secret key. Checking the tag proves the message was not changed and came from someone who knows the key. HMAC is a MAC built from a cryptographic hash function such as MD5 or SHA-1.

The RFC lists the goals of the design. Use existing hash functions without modifying them, especially the ones that already run well in software. Keep the hash function's original speed. Handle keys simply. Have a security analysis that rests on reasonable assumptions about the hash. And make the hash easy to replace when a faster or stronger one appears.

A specific use of HMAC is named after its hash, for example HMAC-SHA1 or HMAC-MD5. The RFC writes the hash function as H.
sections.plainLanguage: HMAC proves that a message was not altered, using a secret both sides share and a hash function that already exists. The design keeps the hash function easy to swap out if a better one is needed later.

sections.title: The HMAC Computation
sections.content:
HMAC assumes a hash function H that works by running a compression function over blocks of data. B is the block length in bytes (B is 64 for MD5, SHA-1 and the other examples the RFC names) and L is the hash output length in bytes (L is 16 for MD5, 20 for SHA-1). The secret key is written K.

Two fixed pads are defined: ipad is the byte 0x36 repeated B times, and opad is the byte 0x5C repeated B times. The letters stand for inner and outer. The whole computation is H(K XOR opad, H(K XOR ipad, text)).

The steps are: pad the key with zero bytes to B bytes; exclusive-OR that block with ipad and append the message, then hash it; exclusive-Or the padded key with opad, append the first hash result, and hash again. The second hash is the output.
sections.plainLanguage: The key is combined with one fixed pattern, and the message is hashed after it. The result is hashed again with the key combined with a different pattern. That second hash is the tag.

sections.title: Keys and Truncated Output
sections.content:
The key may be any length. Keys longer than B bytes are first hashed with H, and the L-byte result becomes the key. Keys shorter than L bytes are strongly discouraged, because they lower the strength of the function. Keys longer than L bytes are acceptable, but the extra length adds little strength, though it may help when the key's randomness is weak.

Keys must be chosen at random, or from a cryptographically strong pseudo-random generator seeded with a random seed, and refreshed periodically. The RFC says current attacks suggest no specific refresh frequency, because those attacks are practically infeasible; refreshing still limits the damage of an exposed key.

An application may truncate the tag, keeping the t leftmost bits of the computation. The RFC recommends t be no less than half the hash output length, to match the birthday attack bound, and no less than 80 bits. A truncated version is written HMAC-H-t, for example HMAC-SHA1-80. When t is not given, the full hash is output.
sections.plainLanguage: Use a long, random key and change it from time to time. You may keep only the first part of the tag, as long as you keep at least half the hash output and at least 80 bits.

sections.title: Implementation Note
sections.content:
HMAC is defined so that the hash function H runs with no code changes, using its own fixed initial value. An implementer who can modify the hash code to accept a variable initial value can gain speed.

The compression function's intermediate results on the blocks K XOR ipad and K XOR opad can be computed once, when the key is generated or before its first use, and stored. Each message then starts from those stored values instead of recomputing them. That saves two compression function calls per message, which matters most for short messages. The RFC stresses that the stored values must be protected exactly like secret keys.

The RFC states that this choice is local to the implementation and has no effect on interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: If you keep reusing the same key, you can do part of the work once in advance and save it. You must guard that saved work as carefully as you guard the key itself.

sections.title: Security of HMAC
sections.content:
The security of HMAC depends on two properties of the hash function: resistance to finding collisions when the initial value is secret and random and the output is not directly available to the attacker, and the message authentication property of the compression function on single blocks. In HMAC those blocks are partly unknown to the attacker, because they contain the result of the inner hash.

The RFC makes two observations about living with imperfect hash functions. The construction depends only on coarse properties of H, so any other secure iterative hash can replace it. And message authentication has a transient effect: if a scheme is broken it gets replaced, but past authenticated information is not exposed. That is unlike encryption, where data encrypted today may be exposed in the future.

The strongest known attack on HMAC is a birthday attack on collisions in H, which the RFC calls totally impractical for any minimally reasonable hash. For MD5, with L equal to 16 bytes (128 bits), the attacker would need correct tags on about 2**64 known plaintexts under the same key, which the RFC calls impossible in any realistic scenario. This differs from ordinary collision attacks on an unkeyed hash, where the same number of parallelizable operations suffice. A note in the introduction records that MD5 had recently been shown vulnerable to collision search attacks, that this did not compromise its use inside HMAC as specified, and that SHA-1 appeared to be the stronger function.
sections.plainLanguage: Breaking the tag would take an enormous amount of work, far beyond any realistic attacker. If a hash is ever broken you switch to a stronger one, and information tagged in the past stays as safe as it was.

data.title: HMAC definition
data.code:
ipad = the byte 0x36 repeated B times
opad = the byte 0x5C repeated B times

HMAC(K, text) = H(K XOR opad, H(K XOR ipad, text))
